confidence_notes: I based the food and drink anchors on four web searches. One was for the RBA rate, and three were for Foz do Iguaçu prices. The price results came from crowdsourced aggregator sites such as traveltables, livingcost, expatistan and citycost. They varied by source and date, and some were from 2023. They put an inexpensive meal at about USD 3-10 (mostly about USD 5.4-5.6), a mid-range dinner for two at about USD 36, a cappuccino at about USD 1.5-1.9 (one Brazilian guide gives R$6-8 for an espresso), and a 0.5 L draught beer at about USD 1.1-1.5. I raised these figures a little to allow for inflation up to July 2026 and for tourist-area restaurant pricing, since a standard serving of draught beer (chopp) in a restaurant is usually 300 ml at about R$10-14. The searches did not turn up reliable aggregated prices for cocktails or wine. Those two anchors are bounded estimates based on how they usually compare with beer in Brazil: a caipirinha typically costs about 2-2.5 times a chopp, and a glass of house wine costs about the same as a cocktail or a little more. The four accommodation anchors are general model estimates only, with no search or listing checks. They allow for a moderate uplift because July is the winter school-holiday peak in Brazil and Argentina. Accommodation, cocktail and wine anchors are less certain than the restaurant and coffee anchors. The BRL/USD rate in July 2026 adds further uncertainty.
comparable_city_reasoning: Mid-sized Brazilian tourist city, similar to Curitiba for food prices, with some tourist uplift near the Falls corridor and hotel strip. Accommodation is benchmarked against other Brazilian leisure destinations with plenty of mid-range stock, like Bonito or Florianópolis outside peak beach season, adjusted for Foz's large and competitive hotel and hostel supply.
